items.stem: Which term describes the methods used to persuade or force individuals to conform to the norms and values of society?
items.answer: Social control
items.markingKey: Social control: the methods used to persuade or force individuals to conform to the norms and values of society. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “negative sanction”, and give one example.
items.answer: A punishment for breaking norms. Example: a detention, a fine or being ignored by friends.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a punishment for breaking norms); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a detention, a fine or being ignored by friends. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “positive sanction” and “agent of social control”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Positive sanction: a reward for conforming to norms (e.g. praise, a prize or a promotion). Agent of social control: a person or institution that enforces norms (e.g. police officers, teachers or parents).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a small village near Kathmandu, a young woman says she would never stay out late because “everyone would talk about it”. Suggest how a radical feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Radical feminism: women are controlled by patriarchy through informal controls such as the fear of violence, gossip and the double standard, as well as through male-dominated formal institutions (Heidensohn).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A school in Jakarta introduces a system of merit points that pupils can exchange for rewards, alongside detentions for lateness. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: women are controlled by patriarchy through informal controls such as the fear of violence, gossip and the double standard, as well as through male-dominated formal institutions (Heidensohn).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of non-participant observation for studying the effects of CCTV on behaviour in public places.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively; a structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); the researcher sees what happens but may not understand the meanings behind it. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of CCTV on behaviour in public places but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes control based on written rules and laws, enforced by official agencies such as the police, courts and prisons?
items.answer: Formal social control
items.markingKey: Formal social control: control based on written rules and laws, enforced by official agencies such as the police, courts and prisons. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “negative sanction”.
items.answer: A punishment for breaking norms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a punishment for breaking norms. [1]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the use of rewards and punishments in schools. Explain one strength of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The interviewer can probe and clarify answers, which improves validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the use of rewards and punishments in schools. [2]

items.stem: A shopping centre in Cairo installs facial-recognition cameras and reports a fall in shoplifting. Explain how functionalist and radical feminist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: social control maintains value consensus and social order; sanctions reinforce shared norms, and limited deviance can even be functional by clarifying boundaries (Durkheim, Parsons). Radical feminism: women are controlled by patriarchy through informal controls such as the fear of violence, gossip and the double standard, as well as through male-dominated formal institutions (Heidensohn).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of sanctions in schools (40 secondary schools, Lima). Table: percentage of schools using this sanction “frequently” | 2015 | 2025. Detentions | 56% | 49%. Merit awards | 47% | 67%. Exclusions | 6% | 6%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Exclusions between 2015 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that schools now rely more on positive than negative sanctions.
items.answer: (a) 6 − 6 = +0 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Merit awards; the figure fell for Detentions; Merit awards had the highest figure for 2025. Foucault might argue that control has become softer but more pervasive. Qualifications: Detentions are still widely used; schools may report the sanctions they think are approved; frequency of use does not show which sanctions are effective. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 40 secondary schools in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 6 and 6; 1 mark for +0 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes behaving in line with the norms and expectations of a group or society?
items.answer: Conformity
items.markingKey: Conformity: behaving in line with the norms and expectations of a group or society. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “crime”, and give one example.
items.answer: Behaviour that breaks the criminal law and can be punished by the state. Example: theft or assault.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (behaviour that breaks the criminal law and can be punished by the state); 1 mark for a relevant example such as theft or assault. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “primary deviance” and “deviant career”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Primary deviance: rule-breaking that has not been labelled and has little effect on a person’s self-identity (e.g. a pupil who occasionally copies homework without being caught). Deviant career: the process by which a person labelled deviant comes to adopt a deviant identity and lifestyle (e.g. a young offender who joins a gang after being rejected by others).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Office workers in Kathmandu secretly take longer breaks than allowed and share jokes about their manager. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: social control works through labelling and interaction: agents of control decide who is deviant, and labels can push people into deviant careers (Becker, Lemert).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Office workers in Cape Town secretly take longer breaks than allowed and share jokes about their manager. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: social control maintains value consensus and social order; sanctions reinforce shared norms, and limited deviance can even be functional by clarifying boundaries (Durkheim, Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Santiago wants to research everyday resistance among workers in a call centre. Evaluate the use of laboratory experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified; the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability. Limitations: the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low; it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying everyday resistance among workers in a call centre but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “primary deviance”.
items.answer: Rule-breaking that has not been labelled and has little effect on a person’s self-identity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: rule-breaking that has not been labelled and has little effect on a person’s self-identity. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “resistance” and “relativity of deviance”?
items.answer: Resistance: actions that challenge or reject the norms, rules or power of dominant groups. Relativity of deviance: the idea that what counts as deviant varies between cultures, over time and between situations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Doha wants to research everyday resistance among workers in a call centre. Explain one strength of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: They can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of everyday resistance among workers in a call centre. [2]

items.stem: Chloe, a 15-year-old in Cape Town, is caught shoplifting once; after a police caution, neighbours call Chloe a “thief” and Chloe begins to spend time with an older group who steal regularly. Explain how functionalist and interactionist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: social control maintains value consensus and social order; sanctions reinforce shared norms, and limited deviance can even be functional by clarifying boundaries (Durkheim, Parsons). Interactionism: social control works through labelling and interaction: agents of control decide who is deviant, and labels can push people into deviant careers (Becker, Lemert).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes agreement among members of society about shared norms and values, so people conform willingly?
items.answer: Consensus
items.markingKey: Consensus: agreement among members of society about shared norms and values, so people conform willingly. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “coercion”, and give one example.
items.answer: The use or threat of force to make people conform. Example: riot police breaking up a protest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the use or threat of force to make people conform); 1 mark for a relevant example such as riot police breaking up a protest. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “rational choice” and “ideological state apparatus”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Rational choice: the view that people conform or deviate after weighing up the likely costs and benefits (e.g. not shoplifting because the risk of being caught is high). Ideological state apparatus: Althusser’s term for institutions that control through ideas, such as education, religion and the media (e.g. school teaching that success is due to individual effort).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A popular film shown in Toronto celebrates a poor young man who becomes a billionaire through hard work and talent. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: conformity results from value consensus: people have internalised shared norms through socialisation and conform willingly, with sanctions used only for the few who deviate (Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A popular film shown in Nairobi celebrates a poor young man who becomes a billionaire through hard work and talent. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: conformity results from coercion and ideology: the state’s repressive apparatus uses force when needed, and institutions spread ideas that legitimate capitalism (Althusser).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: During a strike at a mine near Manila, police in riot gear arrest picket leaders, while newspapers describe the strikers as “selfish”. Compare how functionalist and New Right sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: conformity results from value consensus: people have internalised shared norms through socialisation and conform willingly, with sanctions used only for the few who deviate (Parsons). New Right: conformity depends on strong social bonds and effective sanctions; when attachment, commitment and belief weaken, deviance increases (Hirschi).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for studying how the media presents strikes and protests.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; they can combine quantitative and qualitative data. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how the media presents strikes and protests but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying why most people obey the law.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why most people obey the law but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the use or threat of force to make people conform?
items.answer: Coercion
items.markingKey: Coercion: the use or threat of force to make people conform. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “ideological state apparatus”.
items.answer: Althusser’s term for institutions that control through ideas, such as education, religion and the media.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Althusser’s term for institutions that control through ideas, such as education, religion and the media. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “repressive state apparatus” and “ideological state apparatus”?
items.answer: Repressive state apparatus: Althusser’s term for state institutions that control through force, such as the police, courts and army. Ideological state apparatus: Althusser’s term for institutions that control through ideas, such as education, religion and the media.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A survey of 450 adults in Doha produced the data below. Table: percentage giving this as their main reason for obeying the law | Under 30 | 30 and over. “Because it is the right thing to do” | 41% | 46%. “Because I might get caught” | 28% | 27%. “Because others would disapprove” | 20% | 20%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Under 30 and 30 and over for “Because it is the right thing to do” (30 and over minus Under 30)?
items.answer: +5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 46 − 41 = +5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: The table shows results from research into reasons for obeying the law, using structured interviews with 400 adults in Lima. Table: percentage giving this as their main reason for obeying the law | Under 30 | 30 and over. “Because it is the right thing to do” | 55% | 62%. “Because I might get caught” | 23% | 19%. “Because others would disapprove” | 11% | 12%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Under 30 and 30 and over for “Because I might get caught”. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that conformity is based mainly on consensus rather than coercion.
items.answer: (a) 19 − 23 = -4 percentage points (30 and over compared with Under 30). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for 30 and over than for Under 30 among “Because it is the right thing to do”, “Because others would disapprove”; the figure is lower for 30 and over than for Under 30 among “Because I might get caught”; “Because it is the right thing to do” had the highest figure for 30 and over. Neo-Marxists would argue that apparent agreement may reflect hegemony rather than genuine consensus. Qualifications: A substantial share cite fear of punishment, supporting coercion explanations; people may give socially desirable answers in interviews; hegemony theory suggests “consent” itself is shaped by ideology. The data also come from structured interviews of 400 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 23 and 19; 1 mark for 4 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

Neo-Marxists would argue that apparent agreement may reflect hegemony rather than genuine consensus. The data also come from structured interviews of 800 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.

items.stem: State one way in which schools exercise social control over pupils.
items.answer: Through labelling of pupils.

items.stem: Explain Foucault’s argument that modern societies control people mainly through surveillance and self-discipline rather than physical punishment, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Foucault used the image of Bentham’s panopticon: people who believe they may be watched discipline themselves, so power works through surveillance. Criticism: Critics argue Foucault exaggerates control and underplays resistance; surveillance can also protect people.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Postmodernism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Yusuf, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on sanctions in schools in Manila. The report was based on 40 secondary schools. Table: percentage of schools using this sanction “frequently” | 2015 | 2025. Detentions | 62% | 59%. Merit awards | 54% | 61%. Exclusions | 5% | 4%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Detentions between 2015 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) (59 − 62) ÷ 62 × 100 = -4.8%. (b) The figure rose for Merit awards; the figure fell for Detentions, Exclusions; Merit awards had the highest figure for 2025.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (59 − 62) ÷ 62 × 100; 1 mark for -4.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: Mei is planning a study of informal social control of young women in a small community. Explain two limitations of using covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. Secretly recording sensitive behaviour without consent raises serious ethical problems of deception and harm. 2. It involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to informal social control of young women in a small community. [4]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which agencies of informal social control encourage conformity.
items.answer: Family: rewards, punishments and emotional ties; peer group: approval, teasing and exclusion; religion: moral codes and fear of sin; media: shaming and representations of acceptable behaviour; workplace: promotion or dismissal.

items.answer: Deviance

items.stem: Outline what Becker meant by arguing that deviance is created when moral entrepreneurs make rules and apply them to particular people.
items.answer: Becker argued powerful groups campaign for new rules and labels, so deviance reflects who has the power to define behaviour.

items.answer: 1. They allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words. 2. Rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data.

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying how teenagers who have been cautioned by the police see themselves.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teenagers who have been cautioned by the police see themselves but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. items.stem: Assess how useful official statistics are for studying how the media presents strikes and protests.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how the media presents strikes and protests but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes control based on the approval or disapproval of others, such as family, friends and the community?
items.answer: Informal social control
items.markingKey: Informal social control: control based on the approval or disapproval of others, such as family, friends and the community. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “negative sanction”?
items.answer: A punishment for breaking norms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a punishment for breaking norms. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between formal and informal social control, using an example of each.
items.answer: Formal control is official, based on written rules and enforced by agencies such as the police and courts (e.g. a prison sentence); informal control is unofficial, based on others’ reactions (e.g. a parent’s disapproval or peers’ teasing).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: The table shows results from research into sanctions in schools, using self-completion questionnaires with 40 secondary schools in Manila. Table: percentage of schools using this sanction “frequently” | 2015 | 2025. Detentions | 64% | 54%. Merit awards | 41% | 60%. Exclusions | 7% | 7%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Merit awards between 2015 and 2025. (b) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Merit awards between 2015 and 2025. Show your working.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 41 and 60; 1 mark for +19 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for (60 − 41) ÷ 41 × 100; 1 mark for 46.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2]

items.stem: In a small village near Lagos, a young woman says she would never stay out late because “everyone would talk about it”. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: social control serves the ruling class: agencies such as the police, law and education protect capitalist interests and spread ideology, so conformity is produced by coercion and false class consciousness (Althusser).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of semi-structured interviews for studying the use of rewards and punishments in schools.
items.answer: Strengths: a core set of questions allows some comparison between interviewees while follow-up questions add depth; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the use of rewards and punishments in schools but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes behaviour that breaks the criminal law and can be punished by the state?
items.answer: Crime
items.markingKey: Crime: behaviour that breaks the criminal law and can be punished by the state. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Deviance always involves breaking the law.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Deviance means breaking social norms; much deviance is not illegal (e.g. rudeness), and laws change over time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain Hall and Jefferson’s argument that youth subcultures are a symbolic form of resistance to ruling-class hegemony, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: The Birmingham CCCS argued working-class youth styles (such as skinheads) resisted capitalism through style, but this resistance was “magical”, not changing their real situation. Criticism: Critics argue the CCCS read too much political meaning into style; many young people join subcultures for fun.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Ethan, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on attitudes to deviant behaviour in Kuala Lumpur. The report was based on 1200 adults. Table: percentage who see having a visible tattoo as “unacceptable” at work | 2000 | 2025. People aged 18-29 | 22% | 16%. People aged 30-59 | 37% | 29%. People aged 60+ | 61% | 55%. By how many percentage points did the figure for People aged 30-59 change between 2000 and 2025?
items.answer: -8 percentage points
items.markingKey: 29 − 37 = -8 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Office workers in Jakarta secretly take longer breaks than allowed and share jokes about their manager. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: social control works through labelling and interaction: agents of control decide who is deviant, and labels can push people into deviant careers (Becker, Lemert).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using participant observation to research how teenagers who have been cautioned by the police see themselves.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; the researcher sees what people actually do in their natural setting, not just what they say, so validity is high. Limitations: the researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”); studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teenagers who have been cautioned by the police see themselves but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the use or threat of force to make people conform?
items.answer: Coercion
items.markingKey: Coercion: the use or threat of force to make people conform. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “repressive state apparatus”.
items.answer: Althusser’s term for state institutions that control through force, such as the police, courts and army.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Althusser’s term for state institutions that control through force, such as the police, courts and army. [1]

items.stem: Explain one strength and one weakness of the consensus explanation of conformity.
items.answer: Strength: explains why most people conform most of the time without force, through socialisation. Weakness: it ignores conflict, inequality and power, and cannot explain resistance; Wrong called it “over-socialised”.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for an explained strength; 2 marks for an explained weakness. [4]

items.stem: Most people in Hanoi pay their taxes on time, even though few are ever investigated by the tax authorities. Suggest how a neo-Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: conformity results from hegemony: ruling-class ideas become “common sense” and win consent, though this is never complete and can be challenged (Gramsci).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A survey of 500 adults in Kuala Lumpur produced the data below. Table: percentage giving this as their main reason for obeying the law | Under 30 | 30 and over. “Because it is the right thing to do” | 44% | 56%. “Because I might get caught” | 26% | 18%. “Because others would disapprove” | 14% | 10%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Under 30 and 30 and over for “Because others would disapprove” (30 and over minus Under 30)?
items.answer: -4 percentage points
items.markingKey: 10 − 14 = -4 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how the media presents strikes and protests. Explain one strength of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: They are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how the media presents strikes and protests. [2]

items.stem: Assess how useful semi-structured interviews are for studying why most people obey the law.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: interviewer bias may still affect answers; follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why most people obey the law but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Nadia, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on reasons for obeying the law in Bangkok. The report was based on 1200 adults. Table: percentage giving this as their main reason for obeying the law | Under 30 | 30 and over. “Because it is the right thing to do” | 51% | 62%. “Because I might get caught” | 23% | 14%. “Because others would disapprove” | 15% | 16%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Under 30 and 30 and over for “Because I might get caught”. (b) Explain one limitation of using structured interviews to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that conformity is based mainly on consensus rather than coercion.
items.answer: (a) 14 − 23 = -9 percentage points (30 and over compared with Under 30). (b) They are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for 30 and over than for Under 30 among “Because it is the right thing to do”, “Because others would disapprove”; the figure is lower for 30 and over than for Under 30 among “Because I might get caught”; “Because it is the right thing to do” had the highest figure for 30 and over. Those citing fear of being caught suggest coercion and deterrence also matter. Qualifications: A substantial share cite fear of punishment, supporting coercion explanations; people may give socially desirable answers in interviews; hegemony theory suggests “consent” itself is shaped by ideology. The data also come from structured interviews of 1200 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 23 and 14; 1 mark for 9 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]
